frontmatter.title: Automated Analytics
frontmatter.subtitle: Software Engineer, Full Stack. PHP, TypeScript, data, messaging and cloud.
frontmatter.author: Chris Garlick

blocks.title: What they're hiring for
blocks.intro: A remote full-stack engineer working a prioritised queue of tickets on an AI-driven marketing, recruitment and business intelligence platform.

items.label: Title
items.value: Software Engineer, Full Stack. Remote

items.label: The company
items.value: AI combined with marketing, recruitment and analysis software: clients automate sales and recruitment campaigns and get business intelligence on their performance

items.label: How work arrives
items.value: Tickets allocated by priority and resolution time: **incidents, problems, projects or changes**

items.label: Reports to
items.value: The Head of Customer Delivery, with all allocated work, and the Chief of Product

items.label: Languages
items.value: Expert in PHP and/or TypeScript / JavaScript

items.label: Frameworks
items.value: Laravel (or CakePHP, Yii, CodeIgniter); React, Angular or Vue; Node (Express, NestJS)

items.label: Data
items.value: MySQL, Postgres, MS SQL, NoSQL (Mongo, DynamoDB, Firestore), Redis / Memcached

items.label: Messaging
items.value: SQS, SNS, Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ, Kafka; Protocol Buffers and MessagePack

items.label: Ops
items.value: CI/CD, infrastructure automation, AWS or Google Cloud, serverless and containers

blocks.title: Read between the lines
blocks.body: **Incidents, problems and changes** are ITIL service-management terms, and you report to **Customer Delivery**. This is a client-facing engineering role: fixing what's broken for customers quickly and calmly matters as much as building new features. The long list of technologies says *adaptable*: they want someone who picks things up fast, not an expert in all of them.

blocks.title: What they want, what to show
blocks.intro: Every line in the advert, with the evidence to bring. Be honest about what you've used and what you've read about.

rows: Priority-based ticket work
How you triage a queue and keep stakeholders informed.
Problem-solving
A hard bug or design problem you broke down and solved.
Communication
Explaining a technical issue to a client or non-technical colleague.
Expert PHP / TypeScript
Laravel apps you've built; typed TypeScript on the front end.
Modern front end
A SPA you built with components and async data loading.
Databases and caching
Schema design, a query you sped up, where you used Redis.
Message buses
Laravel queues, or any async job or event system you've run.
REST APIs and security
An authenticated API you designed: tokens, validation, rate limits.
CI/CD and cloud
A pipeline you built; something you deployed to AWS or similar.
Git in a fast team
Your branching, review and conflict-handling habits.

blocks.title: Your strongest stories
blocks.body: **PHP / Laravel**: years of it, which covers the core of the stack. **Typeset**: an API you built and run in production, with a front end, deploys and real operational problems (memory limits on a small server). **Claude Code**: you use AI tools daily, which suits a company built on AI.

blocks.title: Incidents, problems, changes and projects
blocks.intro: The advert uses ITIL language. Knowing the difference shows you understand service delivery.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: **Allocating on a priority based resolution time tickets that need to be completed. These may be: incidents, problems, projects or changes.** Expect a question on how you'd prioritise.

rows: Incident
Something is broken or degraded for a client now
Restore service fast; a workaround counts
Problem
The underlying cause of one or more incidents
Find and fix the root cause so it doesn't recur
Change
A planned change to a live system
Deliver it safely: tested, reviewed, with a rollback
Project
A larger piece of new work
Break it into deliverable pieces; report progress
**High impact** (many clients, revenue, data)
P1: drop everything
P2: today
**Low impact** (one user, a workaround exists)
P3: this week
P4: when there's time

items.title: Triage first
items.detail: Check new tickets for P1s before carrying on with anything else.

items.title: Acknowledge
items.detail: Tell the reporter you have it and when they'll hear next, within the SLA.

items.title: Communicate
items.detail: Update the ticket as you go. Silence is what upsets clients, not the bug.

items.title: Close properly
items.detail: Confirm the fix with the reporter; link incidents to the problem behind them.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"I'd restore service first and investigate second. Once the client is unblocked, I'd raise a problem ticket for the root cause so we fix it once rather than handling the same incident again."*

blocks.title: The five skills they list first
blocks.intro: The advert lists these as *duties*, before any technology. Have one short story for each.

rows: Problem-solving
Break a complex problem down; find a new solution
A bug you couldn't reproduce at first, and how you narrowed it down
Communication
Explain technical ideas to technical and non-technical people
Explaining an outage or a trade-off to a client in plain words
Collaboration
Work well in a team
Code review you gave or received that improved the result
Adaptability
Learn new technology fast; handle changing requirements
A technology you picked up for a project (Typeset is in Rust)
Time management
Juggle priorities and meet deadlines
A week with an urgent fix landing on top of planned work

blocks.title: Structure every story the same way
blocks.body: **Situation** (one sentence), **task** (what you had to do), **action** (what *you* did, the longest part), **result** (what changed, with a number if you can). Two minutes, no more.

blocks.text: Explaining something technical to a non-technical person

items: Start with what it means for them: *"Reports were showing yesterday's numbers."*
Then the cause in one plain sentence: *"The job that refreshes them got stuck."*
Then what happens next and when: *"It's fixed, and we've added an alert so we'll know first next time."*
Leave out the jargon unless they ask for it.

blocks.title: PHP and Laravel
blocks.intro: Your strongest ground. Be ready to go deep.

rows: PHP 8
Typed properties, constructor promotion, enums, match, readonly, named arguments, attributes.
Eloquent
Relationships; eager-load with with() to avoid N+1; scopes; casts; chunk() for big sets.
Queues and jobs
Push slow work (emails, exports, API calls) onto queues; retries, backoff, failed jobs, Horizon on Redis.
Events
Events and listeners to decouple; queue the listeners that are slow.
APIs
API resources for output, Form Requests for validation, Sanctum for tokens, rate limiting middleware.
Testing
Feature tests with RefreshDatabase; fakes for Queue, Mail, Http; Pest or PHPUnit.
Other frameworks
CakePHP, Yii and CodeIgniter share the same MVC ideas: routes, controllers, models, views.

blocks.title: TypeScript and asynchronous UI
blocks.intro: The other half of *expert in PHP or TypeScript*, and the *asynchronous UI development patterns* they list.

rows: Types
Interfaces vs type aliases; unions and narrowing; generics; strict mode on.
Utility types
Partial, Pick, Omit, Record; unknown instead of any for untrusted data.
Promises
async / await; Promise.all for parallel work, allSettled when some may fail.
Event loop
One thread; awaiting yields so the UI stays responsive.
Race conditions
A slow old request overwriting a newer one: cancel with AbortController.
Debounce
Wait until typing stops before searching, so you don't fire a request per key.
UI states
Every async view has four: loading, error, empty and success.
Optimistic updates
Show the change at once, roll back if the server rejects it.

blocks.title: SPA, PWA, components, MVP and MVVM
blocks.intro: They want a *desire to stay current*. Be able to define each term and say when you'd use it.

rows: SPA
One page that loads once; JavaScript renders views and fetches data
App-like dashboards, like a BI or campaign tool
PWA
A web app with a manifest and a service worker: installable, works offline, can push notifications
Users on mobile or patchy connections; no app store needed
Components
UI built from small, reusable pieces with props in and events out
Always; it's how React, Vue and Angular work
MVP
Model, View, Presenter: a passive view; the presenter handles logic and updates the view
Testable UI logic with a thin view
MVVM
Model, View, ViewModel: the view binds to the view model's state and updates automatically
Data-binding frameworks: Vue and Angular are close to MVVM

items.label: SPA trade-offs
items.value: Fast after the first load, but a slower first paint and harder SEO; server rendering (Nuxt, Next) or Inertia helps.

items.label: Service worker caching
items.value: Cache first for static assets; network first for API data so it's never stale.

items.label: State
items.value: Keep state local until it's shared; then a store (Pinia, Redux, Zustand). Server data in a query cache (TanStack Query).

items.label: Laravel + SPA
items.value: Inertia.js gives a SPA feel with Laravel routing and no separate API.

blocks.title: SQL, NoSQL and caching
blocks.intro: They list almost every kind of database. Show you know which to choose and why.

rows: MySQL / Postgres
Relational data, joins, transactions, reporting
Indexes, slow queries on big tables
MS SQL
The same ideas in the Microsoft world; T-SQL
Syntax differences: TOP, not LIMIT
MongoDB
Flexible documents; nested data read together
No joins by default; design for your queries
DynamoDB
Huge scale, single-digit millisecond reads by key
Design partition keys around access patterns up front
Firestore
Real-time sync to web and mobile clients
Query limits; cost per read
Redis
Cache, queues, sessions, counters, rate limits, pub/sub
It's in memory: set TTLs, plan for eviction
Memcached
A simple, fast key-value cache
No persistence and no data structures

items.label: Cache-aside
items.value: Read the cache; on a miss, read the database and store the result with a TTL. Laravel's Cache::remember does this.

items.label: Invalidation
items.value: Delete or update the key when the data changes; use tags or versioned keys for groups.

items.label: Stampede
items.value: Many requests miss at once and all hit the database; use a lock so only one rebuilds the value.

blocks.content:
-- Click-through rate by campaign, last 7 days
SELECT c.name,
       SUM(s.impressions) AS impressions,
       SUM(s.clicks)      AS clicks,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(s.clicks)
             / NULLIF(SUM(s.impressions), 0), 2) AS ctr
FROM campaigns c
JOIN campaign_stats s ON s.campaign_id = c.id
WHERE s.date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 7 DAY
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY ctr DESC;

blocks.title: Message buses and queues
blocks.intro: SQS, SNS, Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ and Kafka. Know the differences and the rules that apply to all of them.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: An automation and analytics platform runs on background work: campaign sends, data imports, report builds. Messaging is how that work is spread out and kept reliable.

rows: SQS
A queue: each message is handled by one consumer
Background jobs on AWS; Laravel's SQS driver
SNS
Publish / subscribe: one message fans out to many subscribers
SNS → several SQS queues, each doing its own job
Google Pub/Sub
Pub/sub with push or pull subscriptions
The same on Google Cloud
RabbitMQ
A broker with exchanges routing to queues
Flexible routing, priorities, work queues
Kafka
A durable, ordered log, split into partitions; consumers replay it
High-volume event streams and analytics pipelines

items.label: At-least-once
items.value: Most systems may deliver a message twice, so consumers must be **idempotent**: processing twice has the same result as once.

items.label: Dead-letter queue
items.value: Messages that keep failing go aside for inspection instead of blocking the queue.

items.label: Ordering
items.value: SQS standard queues don't guarantee order; SQS FIFO and Kafka (within a partition) do.

items.label: Visibility timeout
items.value: In SQS, a message hides while being processed; if the worker dies, it reappears.

items.label: Backpressure
items.value: Watch queue depth and message age; scale workers on them.

rows: JSON
Text, self-describing
Readable, universal; but larger and slower to parse
MessagePack
Binary JSON: same data model, no schema
Smaller and faster, drop-in for JSON
Protocol Buffers
Binary with a schema in .proto files; code generated per language
Compact, typed, versioned; used by gRPC

blocks.title: Protobuf schema evolution
blocks.body: Never reuse or renumber a field tag; add new fields as optional; mark removed ones `reserved`. That keeps old and new services able to read each other's messages.

blocks.title: REST, GraphQL and API security
blocks.intro: Designing and building RESTful APIs, loose familiarity with GraphQL, and API security best practice.

rows: Resources and verbs
GET /campaigns, POST /campaigns, PATCH /campaigns/42, DELETE /campaigns/42
Status codes
Pagination
Cursor-based for large or changing lists; limit the page size
Versioning
/v1/ in the path or a header; never break existing clients
Idempotency
PUT and DELETE are idempotent; an Idempotency-Key header makes POST safe to retry
Consistency
One error format, one date format (ISO 8601), consistent naming

items.label: GraphQL
items.value: One endpoint; the client asks for exactly the fields it needs. Good for complex front ends; harder to cache. Watch for N+1 queries (use DataLoader) and limit query depth.

rows: Broken object-level authorisation
The top API risk: check the user may see *this* record, not just that they're logged in. Laravel policies.
Broken authentication
Short-lived tokens, OAuth 2 for third parties, hashed API keys, HTTPS only.
Mass assignment
Validate and whitelist fields; $fillable in Laravel.
Injection
Parameterised queries; validate all input.
Abuse
Rate limiting per user and per key; size limits on requests.
Data exposure
Return only the fields needed (API resources); never leak stack traces.
Multi-tenancy
Every query scoped to the client's account; test that one client can't see another's data.

blocks.title: CI/CD, infrastructure as code and cloud native
blocks.intro: *Familiarity* and *understanding* are the words they use: you don't need to be an ops engineer.

items.title: On every push
items.detail: Install (cached), lint, static analysis (PHPStan, tsc), unit and feature tests.

items.title: On merge
items.detail: Build once: a Docker image or bundle. Deploy it to staging and run smoke tests.

items.title: To production
items.detail: Promote the same artefact; migrations first; health check; easy rollback.

rows: Terraform
Declares infrastructure in code for any cloud; plan, then apply
CloudFormation / CDK
AWS's own; CDK lets you write it in TypeScript
Ansible
Configures servers by running tasks over SSH
Docker
Packages the app and its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere
AWS Lambda / Cloud Functions
A function per event; pay per run
Webhooks, file processing, scheduled jobs, queue consumers
AWS App Runner / Cloud Run
A container, scaled automatically, even to zero
Web apps and APIs without managing servers
App Engine
Your code on Google's managed platform
Simple web apps

blocks.title: Serverless trade-offs
blocks.body: Cold starts, time limits (15 minutes on Lambda), and database connections (use RDS Proxy). For PHP on Lambda, **Bref** is the usual route; Laravel Vapor is built on it.

blocks.title: Git in a fast-moving team
blocks.intro: They ask for *expertise*. Show habits, not just commands.

rows: Short-lived branches
Merge within a day or two; fewer, smaller conflicts.
Trunk-based or GitHub flow
main is always deployable; feature flags for unfinished work.
Small PRs
Faster, better reviews; easier to revert.
Good commit messages
Say *why*; the diff already says what.
Rebase your branch, don't rewrite shared history
Rebase onto main before merging; never force-push a shared branch.
Revert, don't reset, in production
git revert makes a new commit that undoes a bad one, safely.

blocks.content:
git switch -c fix/ctr-divide-by-zero
git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main  # stay current
git add -p                    # stage only what belongs
git commit -m "Don't divide by zero with no impressions"
git push --force-with-lease   # safe after a rebase

# Find the commit that broke it
git bisect start <bad> <good>
# Undo a bad commit that's already in main
git revert <sha>
# When did this code change?
git log -S "ctr" --oneline

blocks.title: AI, automation and analytics
blocks.intro: Show interest in what they actually build: campaign automation and business intelligence for sales and recruitment.

items.label: Campaign automation
items.value: Scheduled and triggered sends across channels, at volume: queues, retries, rate limits from providers, and unsubscribes respected.

items.label: Integrations
items.value: Ad platforms, CRMs, job boards and ATS systems: OAuth, webhooks, API limits, and data that arrives late or twice.

items.label: Analytics pipeline
items.value: Events collected, cleaned and aggregated into daily tables, so dashboards read summaries, not raw events.

items.label: Accuracy
items.value: "Accurate and fast" is their promise: timezones, duplicates and late data are where numbers go wrong.

items.label: AI features
items.value: Likely scoring, summarising or generating content: structured output, cost and latency, and checking quality.

items.label: Data protection
items.value: Candidate and customer data is personal data under UK GDPR: access control, retention and consent.

blocks.title: A good question to ask yourself before the interview
blocks.body: Look at their website and pick one feature. How would you build it? What would break at 10× the volume? Being able to say that in the interview shows real interest.

blocks.title: Say this
blocks.body: *"What I like about this role is the mix: client-facing tickets where you see the impact straight away, plus the data and automation side, which is where AI is most useful."*

items: Three tickets arrive at once: an outage for one client, a bug for many, and a change due today. What order, and why?
What's the difference between an incident and a problem?
How would you stop a Laravel page making hundreds of database queries?
Explain how you'd handle a search box that fires a request on every keystroke.
What's the difference between a SPA and a PWA? Between MVP and MVVM?
When would you choose DynamoDB or Mongo over MySQL?
SQS and Kafka: what's the difference, and when would you use each?
A message might be delivered twice. How do you make that safe?
How would you secure a REST API used by many client companies?
Describe a CI/CD pipeline you'd set up for a Laravel and Vue app.
How do you undo a bad commit that's already in main?
Tell me about a complex problem you solved.
Explain something technical you worked on as if I weren't a developer.
Tell me about a technology you had to learn quickly.
How do you manage competing priorities and deadlines?
Why Automated Analytics?

blocks.title: Questions to ask them
blocks.intro: Pick three or four that fit the conversation.

items: What's the split between incidents and changes versus project work, week to week?
How are priorities and resolution times set, and who decides when they conflict?
How does working with both Customer Delivery and the Chief of Product work in practice?
What does the stack look like today: which of the technologies in the advert are in use?
Where does AI sit in the product, and what's next for it?
What does the path from commit to production look like? How often do you deploy?
What's the biggest technical challenge the platform has right now?
How big is the engineering team, and how do you work together remotely?
What would success look like in the first three and six months?
How do you support people learning new technologies?

blocks.title: Closing line
blocks.body: *"I'm a strong PHP and Laravel developer who's comfortable across the stack and picks up new tools quickly. I like owning a ticket from the client's report to the fix in production, and keeping people informed along the way. I think I'd fit well here."*

items.title: Look them up
items.detail: Automated Analytics' product, clients and recent news; who's interviewing you.

items.title: Rehearse five stories out loud
items.detail: One for each skill they list: problem-solving, communication, collaboration, adaptability, time management.

items.title: Know your gaps
items.detail: Which listed technologies you've used, and which you've only read about. Say so honestly, then say how you'd learn.

items.title: Practise the definitions
items.detail: Incident vs problem, SPA vs PWA, MVP vs MVVM, SQS vs Kafka, out loud.

items.title: Re-read the advert
items.detail: Its words are your vocabulary: *priority, resolution time, incidents, problems, changes*.

items.title: Check your setup
items.detail: Camera, sound, a working editor and terminal in case of a live exercise.

items.title: Have this guide open
